filedesc.updatestmt:
The William Blake Archive is pleased to announce the publication of five etchings and engravings by William Blake: Christ Trampling on Satan, Lear and Cordelia, Two Afflicted Children, Two Views of an Afflicted Child, and Coin of Nebuchadnezzar and Head of Cancer. With these publications we have completed the category of Separate Prints and Prints in Series, Designed by Blake and Engraved by Other Engravers.
The production of all but the last of the plates named above is associated with the family of Blake's patron, Thomas Butts (1757-1845). Early in 1806, Blake began to teach drawing and engraving to Butts' son, Thomas Butts, Jr. (1788-1862). As receipts indicate, payment for these lessons extended from 3 March 1806 to 14 January 1808, but instruction might have continued a little longer. Although unsigned, the history of the copperplate of Christ Trampling on Satan and the provenances and inscriptions on several impressions of Lear and Cordelia firmly associate these works with the Butts family and the skills young Thomas learned from Blake. Both are based on extant drawings by Blake. The preservation of four states of Lear and Cordelia allows us to trace the development of the plate from early proof to finished (or almost finished) print. These are presented in the Archive as Copies 1 through 4.
Many of the hatching strokes in these prints indicate the work of an amateur, but their attribution to the younger Butts is complicated by two factors. We can expect that a drawing and engraving instructor would participate directly in a new pupil's early efforts. It would not be surprising if Blake outlined the major features of the design on the copperplate and perhaps cut a few demonstration strokes as part of his lessons. Thus, all of the plates attributable to Butts Jr. may have touches from Blake's own hand, however slight. Further, there is a Butts family tradition that the father profited more than the son from Blake's lessons. We are unable to determine if the elder Butts added his own efforts to these plates.
Although Two Afflicted Children and its similar companion, Two Views of an Afflicted Child, look like illustrations for a medical text, the history of the only known impressions associate them with the Butts family. The evidence for Blake's involvement in designing these odd images is admittedly slight, but they are included in the Archive for the sake of completeness and in the hope that further research will clarify their attribution.
The two images in Coin of Nebuchadnezzar and Head of Cancer, known only in a single unsigned impression probably engraved by John Linnell, are definitely attributable to Blake as their designer. The profile is based on one of Blake's Visionary Heads, drawn c. 1819, and is in part a self-portrait. The engraving, however, is associated with the production of illustrations for John Varley's A Treatise on Zodiacal Physiognomy, published in 1828 and also available in the Archive. Varley planned to issue further installments of his booklet, but only the first was published. Coin of Nebuchadnezzar and Head of Cancer was very probably intended for inclusion in one of these unpublished volumes.
As always, the William Blake Archive is a free site, imposing no access restrictions and charging no subscription fees. The site is made possible by the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with the University of Rochester, the continuing support of the Library of Congress, and the cooperation of the international array of libraries and museums that have generously given us permission to reproduce works from their collections in the Archive.

objtitle.title: Coin of Nebuchadnezzar and Head of Cancer

objdescid.origination: John Varley delineator. Although this plate is unsigned, Varley may have played a role in copying Blake's drawings in preparation for their etching and engraving.

John Linnelldelineator, etcher, engraver. Although unsigned, this plate may have been etched and engraved by Linnell, like the plates published in John Varley's *A Treatise on Zodiacal Physiognomy* of 1828. Linnell also may have played a role in copying Blake's drawings in preparation for their etching and engraving.
objdescid.compdate: c. 1828The date is based on the probability that this plate was intended to be included in some future (but never published) installment of John Varley's *A Treatise on Zodiacal Physiognomy*, the first and only published issue of which is dated 1828.

objinfo.objsize: 10.4 x 20.4 cm.The coin on the left measures 10.4 x 11.0 cm.; the profile on the right measures 9.0 x 7.4 cm.
objinfo.platemark: The platemark's vertical dimension is 15.8 cm. The platemark has been trimmed off on the right and left margins in the only known impression.

provenance.note: John Linnell, who may have engraved the plate c. 1828; according to Geoffrey Keynes, *Bibliotheca Bibliographici* (London: Trianon Press, 1964) 86, no. 611, this impression was sold from the Linnell collection, Christie's, 15 March 1918, included in lot 190, "a parcel" of "Blake (William) Engravings" (£54.12s. to the dealer A. Martin, possibly acting for W. E. Moss); sold from the Moss collection, Sotheby's, 2 March 1937, lot 216 (£1.5s. to Keynes); given by Keynes by bequest in 1982 to the Fitzwilliam Museum, which accessioned the work in 1985.

desc.objtitle: Coin of Nebuchadnezzar and Head of Cancer, Object 1 (Essick LVII)

objnote.p: The only known impression of this separate plate, reproduced here, is without inscriptions and thus is probably a proof to which captions or other lettering would be added in a published state. The identification of the figure on the coin (left image) as Nebuchadnezzar is based on the inscription on a tracing of Blake's original drawing, now lost. The other side of the coin is pictured in John Varley's *A Treatise on Zodiacal Physiognomy* of 1828, Object 3 in the Archive. The identification of the profile on the right as a person representing or born under the traditional astrological sign of Cancer is based on Blake's drawing of the profile, inscribed "Cancer," and the similarity between this profile and a portrait labeled "Cancer" in Varley's *Treatise*, Object 1 in the Archive. See the introductory essay for further discussion.

illustration.illusdesc: A coin featuring the face of Nebuchadnezzar in profile is located left of center on this plate, while the face of a man representing or born under the traditional astrological sign of Cancer, also in profile, appears on the right. The coin is round with an uneven surface and rough edges, with the male face of Nebuchadnezzar depicted looking left. He has long hair and wears a crown. The odd, jagged forms in front of Nebuchadnezzar's face might suggest either inscriptions on the coin or bolts of lightning. Cancer's head and neck appear in profile, looking left.

component.illusobjdesc: A coin featuring the face of Nebuchadnezzar in profile is located left of center on this plate. The coin is roughly circular, round with an uneven surface and rough edges. Nebuchadnezzar looks left; his left eye is opened wide. He may be staring at something off to the left that frightens him. He has a prominent ear, long hair, and a beard and wears a spiky crown. Around the left edge of the coin, a series of jagged designs or marks might be an inscription or possibly bolts of lightning.

On the right, another male figure's head and neck appear in profile. This is Blake's physiognomic representation of the zodiac sign of Cancer. The figure has a prominent forehead and furrowed brow and looks left. He has a large left ear, a thick neck, and long but somewhat thin hair.
